blocks.html: On August 3, as the public was first learning about Professor Jason Arday, then of the Cambridge Faculty of Education and Jesus College, Tyler Austin Harper posted a thread challenging the way elite institutions have approached the hiring and promotion of black scholars. In his view, the leaders of these schools frequently select mediocre academics for symbolically important “first-ever” positions, while passing over “*actual* black heavy hitters.” Harper’s claim naturally leads to the question: if not only to elevate those members of the academic community who demonstrate talent, hard work, and good, collegial character, which other overt and tacit dependencies determine these disappointing choices? Harper alludes to two kinds. “There are plenty of talented black academics, and these elite schools step over their bodies to elevate scrubs who either come from rich families ([Claudine] Gay) or who let them feel the warm glow of the white man’s burden (Arday).”

Claudine Gay’s rise to the presidency of Harvard University cannot be understood without the context of her family wealth and long experience socializing among elites, beginning with her prep school education at one of Harvard’s oldest feeders. But I am guessing Harper would agree that Harvard’s old guard elevated Gay to the presidency not for her family background per se but rather because she offered an attractive two-for-one deal: a black woman who also has a large network of politically valuable personal connections, probably thoughtfully maintained. Gay is a shrewd operator and undoubtedly a talent in her field—not academia, that is, but politics. Remember, this is Harvard. Some of its leadership, observing hundreds of millions in federal money flowing through its budget each year, were perhaps not totally nuts in thinking the university would do well with a politician instead of a scholar at its head.
